description:
I’m Zineb Naimi, PM & Science Lead for "The Moon’s Silent Witnesses" (NASA Space Apps). We're tackling "Abandoned but Not Forgotten" with a team-first mindset!

Looking for 5 teammates (ages 14–21): Science/Data Co-Lead, Storyteller, UI/UX Designer, Web/App Dev & Video Editor. Join us!
summary: The Moon's Silent Witnesses is an educational and interactive web designed for children aged 10 to 14 to make complex space science easy and fun. Official space archives are packed with heavy technical jargon that discourages young learners. Our solution transforms this complicated data into an engaging adventure: an interactive lunar map featuring five real abandoned rovers and landers. When a kid clicks on a robot, we give it a voice and a personality, turning a cold machine into a living storyteller that explains its mission and composition in simple terms. To ensure everyone understands, the app features a dual-level explanation system (with an even simpler version if needed) and an interactive final quiz. Why it is important: By turning difficult science into child's play and giving these machines a voice, we prove they are abandoned, but never forgotten—preserving space history while inspiring the next generation of young engineers.
details:
The Moon's Silent Witnesses is an interactive educational web application designed for children aged 10 to 14 to make complex space science accessible, easy, and fun. Upon opening the app, users are immersed in an interactive lunar map dotted with five markers representing real historic, abandoned landers, rovers, and probes on the Moon. A friendly voice guide welcomes the explorer and invites them to click on any marker. When clicked, the camera zooms in and the robot comes to life through integrated voice-over narration with its own personality, explaining its mission, history, and material composition in simple terms. After the story, a dual-level explanation system engages the user: if a concept feels too complicated, clicking "No" prompts the robot to offer an ultra-simple, relatable breakdown. Once understood, clicking "Yes" launches a gamified final quiz to test knowledge and reward exploration.

The project bridges the gap between official, jargon-heavy space agency archives and young learners. Its intended impact is twofold: first, it rescues forgotten lunar hardware from obscurity, preserving space exploration heritage and proving that while these machines are physically abandoned on the Moon, they are never forgotten. Second, it empowers the next generation of scientists and engineers by turning difficult aerospace engineering into child's play through storytelling and gamification.

To develop this solution, our team utilized verified open-access space mission data, landing coordinates, and historical archives from NASA and international space agencies, building the app using modern web technologies (HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript) alongside pre-integrated audio and text-to-speech tools for voice-acted storytelling, plus Prezi for our presentation. Our project is creative because it treats historic spacecraft not as cold metal artifacts, but as living characters with stories to tell. As a team, we carefully considered user experience for children, ensuring high accessibility, avoiding intimidating technical barriers, and maintaining historical validity while keeping the learning journey magical.
